one_liner: Constexpr C++20 template library for IEEE half to octuple floats; inlined Quad beats libquadmath on add/mul/fma/sqrt/casts, loses on div/exp/log/pow.
what_it_does: TLFloat provides IEEE 754 types Half, BFloat16, float, double, Quad (binary128) and Octuple (binary256) as trivially copyable C++ classes with the same bit layout as the IEEE format, plus most of math.h (trig, exp/log, pow, erf, tgamma, rounding) and printf/strtod-style I/O. The C++20 API (tlfloat/tlmath.hpp) is header-only, constexpr and needs no malloc or libstdc++; a separate C/C++11 API (tlfloat/tlfloat.h, link -ltlfloat) offers tlfloat_quad/tlfloat_octuple and an optional libquadmath emulation layer (define TLFLOAT_LIBQUADMATH_EMULATION to get sinq, powq, strtoflt128, quadmath_snprintf etc. on clang and MSVC). It also exposes its BigUInt<N>/BigInt<N> 2^N-bit integer templates for general use.
how_it_is_fast: Each float is unpacked into sign, exponent and an integer mantissa held in a recursive BigUInt<N> template (two 2^(N-1)-bit halves), and arithmetic is done as fixed-width integer operations that use x86 intrinsics (_addcarry_u64, _umul128, inline-asm divq, __builtin_clzll) or __int128 when available, with Karatsuba only at 1024+ bits and Newton-style reciprocal approximations for division and sqrt. With TLFLOAT_ENABLE_INLINING every operation is marked always_inline, so the compiler can inline the whole soft-float path into the caller's loop instead of calling an out-of-line routine; the benchmark builds TLFloat this way (--inline-limit=1000000) while libquadmath functions remain shared-library calls.
when_to_use: You need IEEE binary128 arithmetic on clang or MSVC, where GCC's __float128/libquadmath is unavailable, and want bit-identical results across Linux, Windows, wasm and CUDA device code.
Inner loops heavy on quad add/mul/compare/rint/casts or fma: the README run shows 1.3-1.4x on add/mul, about 5x on rint and about 35x on fma versus libquadmath on a Ryzen 9 7950X.
Compile-time evaluation of high-precision constants or tables (all C++20 functions are constexpr), or freestanding/microcontroller targets with no malloc.
You need octuple (binary256) precision with correctly rounded basic operations and 1-ulp elementary functions, where no hardware or compiler type exists.
when_not_to_use: Division- or transcendental-heavy quad code on GCC/x86-64: libquadmath was faster on div (72.6 vs 50.8 Mops/s), atan (3.02 vs 1.30), exp, log and pow in the same run.
Arbitrary or run-time-selected precision: widths are fixed by template parameters (BigUInt sizes are powers of two), so it does not replace MPFR/GMP.
Code that relies on non-default rounding modes or floating-point exception flags: neither is documented for TLFloat.
Throughput-oriented SIMD work: the project's wiki says it prioritizes accuracy and portability over throughput, unlike its sibling SLEEF.
Projects that cannot use C++20 for the header API (the C++11 API is non-constexpr and requires linking the built library).

integration.form: header-only (C++20 API) or static/shared lib (C and C++11 API, -ltlfloat)
integration.dependencies: none for the library; MPFR optionally for testers and table generation; libquadmath only for the comparison benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for tlmath.hpp/tlfloat.hpp (README example uses g++ -std=c++20); C++11 or C for tlfloat.h; CMake 3.16+ to build; CUDA 12+ for device use with --expt-relaxed-constexpr
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows (MSVC, clang-cl), microcontrollers, wasm and CUDA per README; x86-64 intrinsics and __int128 paths used where available, portable C++ otherwise; big-endian supported since v1.8.0; a ppc64el build failure (issue #4) was closed in Feb 2026
integration.thread_safety: README: 'All functions are thread-safe and reentrant'
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: with TLFLOAT_LIBQUADMATH_EMULATION and tlfloat.h most libquadmath functions (sinq, powq, strtoflt128, quadmath_snprintf) map onto TLFloat, but that path goes through the out-of-line C library; the benchmarked speed comes from the C++20 tlfloat::Quad type, a different interface

gotchas: The published speedups come from the header-only C++ Quad built with forced inlining; the C/libquadmath-emulation API calls into libtlfloat and was not benchmarked against libquadmath in the README (the C-API bench target is only built when the compiler lacks __float128).

In bench.cpp the 'libquadmath' add, mul, div, compare and cast rows apply plain operators to GCC __float128, so they time GCC's compiler-provided soft-float routines rather than libquadmath functions; only fma, sqrt, rint, sin, atan, exp, log and pow call libquadmath.
The README numbers are from TLFloat 1.11.0, while the current CMakeLists.txt declares 1.17.1, and the optimization flags of the published run (e.g. -march=native) are not stated.

Building the library or tests sets very high constexpr step limits (-fconstexpr-ops-limit=1000000000 on GCC, /constexpr:steps1000000000 on MSVC); heavy constexpr use in your own code may need the same flags.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TLFloat over simd-f128 (whose README tables against __float128 disagree with each other) when you want a full IEEE binary128/binary256 math library with correctly rounded basic operations and portability to MSVC/CUDA; pick DoubleFloats.jl or MultiFloats.jl instead for faster ~106-bit double-double arithmetic in Julia when non-IEEE semantics are acceptable, and MPFR-based entries (LibBF, FLINT) when precision must exceed 237 bits or vary at run time.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own bench tool (src/util/bench.cpp, -DBUILD_BENCH=True) times 256-element loops of each operation for 10 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X at 4.5 GHz with gcc 12.3.0: TLFloat 1.11.0 Quad (inlined) beat GNU libquadmath / GCC __float128 on add (124 vs 88 Mops/s), mul (102 vs 78), compare, casts to/from double (168 vs 64), sqrt (15.9 vs 9.5), rint (191 vs 38), fma (68.5 vs 1.9) and sin (2.13 vs 1.77), and lost on div, atan, exp, log and pow. First-party, single machine, flags beyond the CMake defaults not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-17, 223 commits, no open issues) by the author of SLEEF under BSL-1.0, with a README request that companies earning over US$1M from it fund maintenance; small but niche (38 stars), with releases on GitHub up to v1.15.0 and a source tree now at 1.17.1.
